analysis.title: [GSX] midterms
key_insights: With under one week to the midterms, the GS FICC & Equities desk (Faris Mourad) argues the more actionable question is which policy areas become easier to negotiate, get more regulatory attention, or gain leverage in future spending debates, rather than which Democratic priorities become law.
The House passed a continuing resolution funding the government through December 11 in a bipartisan vote, avoiding a shutdown into November.
Affordability is a common theme across Democratic and Republican agendas. The desk lays out equity expressions for each affordability area.

ACA: the enhanced premium tax credits expired at the end of 2025, which led to higher premiums and lower marketplace participation. Providers face rising bad debt and uncompensated care as patients move to self-pay. The desk is long the ACA-exposed beneficiaries basket (GSHLCACA), recently rebalanced.

Drug pricing: both parties emphasize Medicare negotiation expansion, MFN benchmark pricing, redefining the exclusivity clock, and stricter Medicaid and PBM obligations. The desk is short the Drug-Makers basket (GSHLCBPH). MRK and AMGN have identified drugs that could face price setting starting in 2028, with a projected decline in US sales.
Tying US drug prices to international benchmarks through Democratic legislation would be 'drastic and unprecedented' according to ALGS filings. The current route is executive order.

Power inflation: the Democratic AI and energy agenda centers on 'ratepayer protection', shifting AI power infrastructure costs from households to datacenters. Datacenter concerns are bipartisan but stronger among Democrats. The desk calls it one of the more underappreciated election-sensitive themes in US equities.

The datacenter debate is shifting from whether to build to who pays for added generation and transmission. Utilities and grid operators could benefit from regulatory clarity, while economics for some datacenter projects become less attractive.
Power trades: long Renewables (GSXURNEW), Grid Infrastructure (GSXUGRID) and Power Up America (GSENEPOW), and buy protection on Hyperscalers (GSXUHYPR) and Datacenter Equipment (GSTMTDAT).

Government spending: Congress has run on continuing resolutions since the end of the Biden administration. Republicans want more defense spending without matching increases elsewhere, while Democrats want parity between defense and domestic. The desk sees scope for broader spending debate before November and around the December CR expiry.

Spending trades: long Government-Spending Exposed ex-Defense and Drug-Makers (GSXUGOVT), recently rebalanced, and short Defense Spending Beneficiaries (GSXUDFNS). Domestic contractors, federal suppliers, grant recipients and research institutions are the primary beneficiaries.

Corporate tax: the 2025 OBBBA made several TCJA business provisions permanent (100% bonus depreciation) alongside the 21% statutory rate. Because Trump can still veto, the midterms are unlikely to change tax law. 2027-28 earnings are largely insulated, and the risk is to valuations beyond 2029.
Antitrust: Democratic leaders have criticized current antitrust enforcement, with potential for stricter Big Tech oversight. The desk is short Big Tech.

Financial regulation: Democrats have focused on rebuilding CFPB authority and Wall Street oversight, which could dampen bullish momentum in Financials. The desk is short Investment Banks and Cryptocurrency-exposed equities.

Tariffs: Democrats would have limited ability to reverse tariffs while Trump is in office and uses alternative authorities after the Supreme Court invalidated the IEEPA tariffs. The desk sees more risk of tariffs rising than falling between now and early 2027 and is short Tariff-Sensitive Equities.

Housing: Congress passed bipartisan housing-supply legislation in 2026. Democrats could differentiate through expanded housing tax credits and first-time homebuyer incentives, but significant fiscal measures need presidential approval. The desk is long Homebuilders.
